title: Gamay
description: Beaujolais' grape: light, juicy and fragrant, from fresh nouveau to serious crus.
L: Gamay, fully Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc, gives light to medium-bodied reds with red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, violet and sometimes banana or bubblegum from winemaking. Tannins are low, acidity fresh. It's pale to medium purple and made to be fresh and drinkable.

Gamay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, from Burgundy. In 1395, Duke Philip the Bold banned it from Burgundy, calling it a very bad and disloyal plant, to protect Pinot Noir. Gamay moved south to Beaujolais, where granite soils suit it far better than Burgundy's limestone.
Why did Gamay move to Beaujolais?
It was banned from Burgundy in 1395
Philip the Bold banned it to protect Pinot Noir; it found a better home on Beaujolais granite.

Look for a bright purple colour, juicy red fruit, often floral notes, and a light, fresh palate with low tannin. Carbonic maceration adds banana or bubblegum. Compared with Pinot Noir, Gamay is usually juicier and simpler, with more purple in the colour.
Gamay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.
Yes. It shares the same parents as Chardonnay.
Gamay gives juicy red fruit, low tannin and fresh acidity
It was banned from Burgundy in 1395 and moved to Beaujolais
It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc

Beaujolais, just south of Burgundy, grows almost all of the world's Gamay. In the south, on clay and limestone, it makes simple Beaujolais. In the north, on pink granite and schist, it makes Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus. Granite drains well and is poor, giving Gamay its best structure and perfume.

Gamay grows in the Loire, in Touraine and Anjou, often for light reds and rosés, and in the Côte Roannaise. Switzerland blends it with Pinot Noir to make Dôle. It's appearing in Oregon, Canada's Niagara and Australia. Burgundy's Coteaux Bourguignons can include it.
Match each place to its Gamay.
Look for cru Beaujolais rather than plain Beaujolais. The ten crus, on granite, show what Gamay can really do, often at modest prices.
Granite is poor, not fertile, and that helps.
Beaujolais grows almost all the world's Gamay
Northern granite gives the best wines
The Loire, Switzerland and Oregon grow some too

In carbonic maceration, whole, uncrushed bunches go into a tank filled with carbon dioxide. Without oxygen, enzymes inside each berry start fermenting sugar into alcohol, up to about 2%, and create aromas like banana, bubblegum and kirsch. Then berries burst, and yeast finishes the job. Colour comes out, but little tannin.

Most Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic maceration. Whole bunches go into the tank; the weight crushes the bottom ones, which ferment normally, producing CO2 that fills the tank. The upper berries undergo carbonic maceration. The result: fruity, soft wines with low tannin. Some crus use traditional crushing for more structure.
What does carbonic maceration typically produce?
Fruity, soft wines with banana or bubblegum notes
Intracellular fermentation gives fruity aromas and little tannin.

Beaujolais Nouveau is made fast, by semi-carbonic maceration, and released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest. It's light, fruity and meant for immediate drinking. Its fame in the 1980s and 1990s made Beaujolais a household name, but also hurt its reputation for serious wine.
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third ____ of November.
The third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.
Carbonic maceration ferments whole berries in CO2
It gives fruity, soft wines with banana and bubblegum notes
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November

Gamay's low tannin and fresh acidity make it very food-friendly. It suits charcuterie, roast chicken, salmon, pâté and Lyon's bistro food, like saucisson and andouillette. It handles light spice better than tannic reds. It's a great picnic wine.

Serve slightly cool, 12 to 14 degrees; a little chill brings out its fruit. Nouveau within months; Beaujolais and Villages within two or three years. Structured crus, like Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, can age 10 years or more, becoming more like Pinot Noir, a process called pinoter.
A slight chill keeps its fruit lively.
Aged Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can taste surprisingly like Burgundy. Locals say the wine pinote, becomes Pinot-like, with age.
Some Beaujolais crus can age 10 years or more.
Yes. Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent are known for ageing well.
Gamay suits charcuterie, chicken and bistro food
Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can age 10 years or more
Who banned Gamay from Burgundy in 1395?
Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, called it a very bad and disloyal plant.
Not true. It's low in tannin, especially with carbonic maceration.
Gamay is pale to medium purple.
Gamay is best served at about ____ degrees.
Gamay is juicy, light and low in tannin
Beaujolais' granite gives its best wines
Carbonic maceration gives fruity, soft styles
Serve it slightly cool with bistro food
